title_en: Kyle Shanahan’s offense: what makes the scheme special? Part 2
teaser_en: Part 2 of the series on Kyle Shanahan’s offense.
body_en:
## Second quarter: the origins of the offense and the basics

## Which coaches influenced Shanahan the most

As his résumé already suggests, the biggest influence on Kyle Shanahan as a coach was probably his father, Mike Shanahan. Especially in the late '80s and the '90s, Mike Shanahan shaped the **outside zone run game** and derived the passing game from this very horizontal movement in the run game, in the form of bootlegs and play-action, which is still a core element of the Shanahan offense today. Especially during the very successful Denver Broncos era with two Super Bowl triumphs, with Terrell Davis at RB and Hall of Fame QB John Elway, Shanahan conjured up an outstanding offense, with the help of his offensive coordinator Gary Kubiak and offensive line coach Alex Gibbs. Indirectly, Bill Walsh, the legendary 49ers coach of the 1980s who won three Lombardi Trophies with the team, also had an influence on Kyle Shanahan as a coach that should not be underestimated. There is no straight line from Bill Walsh's coaching tree to Kyle Shanahan, but his father succeeded Mike Holmgren as the 49ers' offensive coordinator and, under Walsh's successor George Seifert, was able to adopt many of the offense's principles. Other well-known coaches such as Andy Reid and Jon Gruden in turn come from the Mike Holmgren tree. The latter, as mentioned, was the first NFL head coach Kyle Shanahan got to work under. Kyle Shanahan then got his first big coordinator job under Gary Kubiak in Houston. Kubiak had already been QB coach with the 49ers under Mike Shanahan in 1994 and followed him to the Denver Broncos, where he was Shanahan's offensive coordinator for many years and, years later, would even win the Super Bowl as head coach. In that sense, Kyle Shanahan could almost be counted as part of Gary Kubiak's coaching tree, as could Kevin Stefanski of the Browns, among others. It all sounds very confusing, but it does become clear that everything in this big coaching family is connected somehow (see the family tree below).

As Kyle Shanahan's career described above shows impressively, he has played a major role in spreading the Shanahan "scheme" far across the NFL, through himself and his former assistants.

![The Shanahan coaching tree](https://i0.wp.com/theninerempiregermany.de/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Coaching-Tree.jpg?resize=639%2C428&ssl=1)

Source: [https://theanalyst.com/2022/02/mike-shanahan-zone-run-blocking-scheme-super-bowl-lvi-los-angeles-rams-cincinnati-bengals/](https://theanalyst.com/2022/02/mike-shanahan-zone-run-blocking-scheme-super-bowl-lvi-los-angeles-rams-cincinnati-bengals/)

## The tactics behind it

## The run game

The **outside zone running game** is the foundation of the Shanahan offense and has been refined over decades. The roots of this philosophy go back to the 1980s, when offensive line gurus developed it further. Mike Shanahan perfected the concept with the Denver Broncos in the 1990s and passed it on to his son Kyle Shanahan, who continues to develop it in the NFL to this day.

The first approaches to zone blocking emerged in the 1960s and 1970s under coaches such as Howard Mudd and Jim McNally. The goal was to develop a flexible run game that relies on mobility instead of strength and creates defensive unpredictability. Instead of winning individual blocking matchups, offensive linemen were to work in zones and define the running back's path only after the snap. A decisive further development came from Alex Gibbs, one of the most renowned offensive line coaches, who in the late 1980s with the Denver Broncos consistently relied on outside zone as the primary run concept. The system demanded not only technical precision from the offensive linemen but also extreme athleticism, so they could move parallel to the line of scrimmage.

When Mike Shanahan became head coach of the Denver Broncos in 1995, he made the outside zone system the centerpiece of his offense. With Alex Gibbs as offensive line coach, he created a run game strategy that stretched defensive fronts horizontally, across the full width of the field, opening cutback lanes for the running back, who could then run through between the blocks. An outstanding example of the system's success is the Terrell Davis era. The outside zone system allowed Davis, a Hall of Fame-caliber running back, to rush for 7,607 yards in only seven years. The system emphasized three crucial reads for the running back: running straight through an emerging gap ("bang"), cutting back through a backside gap ("bend") or bouncing outside when the defense clogs the middle ("bounce"). With two Super Bowl wins (1997 and 1998), the zone blocking system became the model for many NFL teams.

While Mike Shanahan perfected the classic zone running game, Kyle Shanahan introduced modern concepts to adapt the system to the changing conditions of the NFL. These include pre-snap motion to manipulate the defense, tight splits for wide receivers to create better blocking angles, and a stronger link to play-action passes.

In addition to the classic outside zone, Kyle Shanahan has begun to integrate more gap-scheme elements. While the classic outside zone scheme is based primarily on zone blocking, power and counter concepts allow even greater variety in the run game. This combination makes defensive adjustments harder to land and the running game less predictable. As a result, the system stays flexible and can respond to different defensive strategies.

## The passing game

The passing game in the Shanahan offense builds on the fundamental principles of the run game. With the Broncos in the '90s, it was still mostly rollouts, where QB John Elway could make perfect use of his combination of a strong arm and an athletic body (like Josh Allen today). In Kyle's early years as a play-caller, it was above all play-action, tight formations and a strong focus on yards after the catch that formed the foundation as well. Over the years there were significant adjustments in response to defensive developments and changing personnel. Particularly striking was the shift in 2024, when dropback passing took on a bigger role (planned or not; keyword "CMC injury") and made the offense more versatile.

As mentioned, in the early years under Kyle Shanahan the passing game was heavily shaped by play-action. With quarterbacks like Jimmy Garoppolo or Nick Mullens, the offense relied on pulling linebackers out of the middle of the field with run fakes and enabling rhythmic, quick passes into the windows that then opened up. The system was also designed to put the quarterback in a comfortable position by using bootleg and rollout concepts to move him out of the pocket and create easy decisions. The interplay between the outside zone run game and play-action made the offense particularly efficient, as shown in the successful 2019 NFC Championship season. A central aspect is timing, the coordination between QB and receiver. Every called pass play should be designed so that the QB has a receiver ready to be thrown to on his route at certain fixed points in his dropback. For example, the QB can throw the short route after the third step, the intermediate route after the fifth step or the deep route after the seventh step. If the player in question is covered at the planned moment, the dropback read process continues and the QB looks to the next potential receiver. It is these play designs that take a lot of responsibility off the quarterback, since he more or less just works through his "paint-by-numbers" set. However, besides quick decisions from the QB, it also requires receivers who stick exactly to the timing of their routes.

From 2022 on, Shanahan responded to the defensive changes brought about by the growing spread of two-high-safety defenses by integrating more spread elements into his system, stretching the field wider. The offense began to rely more often on 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) and to use empty formations (no RB in the backfield) to identify defensive coverages early.

In addition, more "choice routes" were introduced, which allow receivers, above all Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle, to adjust their route flexibly depending on the coverage. These changes made the passing game more varied, but play-action remained a central part of the system.

Probably the biggest change came in 2024, when Shanahan integrated dropback passing more strongly into his offense. Until then, his system had been heavily geared toward relieving the quarterback through play design and giving him clear reads. But with Brock Purdy's development as a quarterback, Shanahan decided to give him more responsibility in the pocket, because he trusted that Purdy could also find answers outside the intended play and was therefore not as dependent on the perfect play call. At the same time, the offensive line was usually stable enough to allow more straight dropback passing without immediate pressure. As a result, the 49ers diversified their passing game and integrated more classic 5- and 7-step dropbacks into their offense. This allowed vertical concepts such as dagger routes and isolated one-on-one situations to be used more effectively to generate explosive plays.

These changes made the offense more versatile and harder to predict. While play-action remained an important element, the passing game became less dependent on it and allowed Shanahan to attack defenses in different ways. Overall, the development of the Shanahan passing game since 2017 shows how the system has continuously adapted to modern defensive schemes. From a play-action-dominated offense with lots of yards after contact, through the integration of spread elements, to the increased use of dropback passing: Shanahan's ability to adapt his system flexibly is a key reason for his offense's long-term success.

Now we know the background of the notorious "Shanahan scheme," but still not really what exactly it means. Hopefully the second half can shed more light on that: third quarter, what is "scheme"?
